greek-yogurt-0pct: Highest protein per kcal of the everyday dairy. Strained, so less calcium per 100 g than regular yogurt. Use as a base for raita, dips and bowls instead of cream.
cottage-cheese-1pct: High protein, very low fat. Salted, so taste before adding more salt. Good cold with fruit or blended into batters and bakes.
milk-whole: Protein, calcium and B12 in an easy form. Fat-soluble vitamins come with the fat, so whole milk suits children and low-appetite days; 2% or skim cuts kcal.
milk-2pct: Same protein and calcium as whole milk with less saturated fat. A sensible default for daily use.
milk-skim: Lowest kcal of the milks with the same protein and calcium. Check that it is vitamin D fortified if it is a main calcium source.
dahi-plain: Fermented, so lactose is easier for many people. Set at home or buy plain with live cultures. Add after cooking: heat kills the cultures.
buttermilk-chaas: Light, hydrating and low kcal. Salted spiced chaas is a good way to add dairy protein with a meal. Watch sodium if you add a lot of salt.
butter-salted: Mostly saturated fat, so use small amounts for flavour. Salted: reduce salt elsewhere in the recipe.
cream-35: Almost all fat. Use a spoonful to finish a dish, not as a base. Yogurt or blended cashews give creaminess with less saturated fat.
cream-18: Lighter than whipping cream but still mostly fat. A small amount finishes curries well.
milk-powder-skim: Concentrated milk protein and calcium. Stir a spoonful into porridge, batters or dough to raise protein without changing taste much.
condensed-milk: A sugar-heavy ingredient: treat dishes made with it as treats. Not used in everyday recipes here.
ricotta-part-skim: Mild and soft, with whey protein. Use fresh within a few days of opening. Works in bakes, stuffings and as a spread.
mozzarella-part-skim: A moderate-fat cheese with good protein. Melt a small amount over bakes; salt is high, so go light elsewhere.
cheddar: Strong flavour, so a little goes far. High in saturated fat and sodium: grate a small amount over a dish rather than slicing.
paneer: Main vegetarian protein and calcium source, but high in fat. Cook it briefly: long cooking toughens it. Soak in warm water for 10 minutes to soften. Low-fat paneer exists.
khoa: Reduced milk solids, rich in fat and kcal. A sweet-making ingredient; keep portions small.
dates-dry: Fibre and potassium with a lot of natural sugar. Eat 2 or 3 with nuts or yogurt to slow the sugar rise, rather than alone.
dates-medjool: Soft and very sweet. Pair with nuts or nut butter. Counted as a free sugar source in this app because they are used to sweeten.
raisins: Concentrated sugar with some iron and potassium. A small handful in oats or salad is plenty.
figs-dried: Good fibre and calcium for a fruit. Sweet, so pair with nuts or yogurt.
apricots-dried: Source of beta-carotene and potassium. Choose unsulphured if you can; they are darker but have no sulphite.
prunes-dried: Well studied for gentle regularity thanks to fibre and sorbitol. Start with a few and see how you tolerate them.
ghee: Stable at high heat and rich in flavour, but pure fat and mostly saturated. A teaspoon on dal or roti is enough.
coconut-meat-raw: High in saturated fat and fibre. Use grated in chutneys and curries for flavour and texture.
coconut-desiccated: Dense in fat and kcal. A spoonful as garnish; unsweetened only.
coconut-milk: Rich and high in saturated fat. Use light coconut milk or dilute it; a splash is enough for flavour in a curry.
besan: High in protein and fibre for a flour. Cook fully: raw besan tastes bitter and is hard to digest. Chilla and pudla are an easy way to use it.
rice-flour: Mostly starch with little protein. Good for crisping batters. Pair with a protein like paneer or dal in the same meal.
arrowroot-flour: Pure starch used as a thickener. Adds no protein or fibre.
banana: Potassium and quick energy. Ripe bananas are sweeter and raise blood sugar faster: pair with peanut butter or yogurt.
apple: Fibre and polyphenols are in the skin, so wash and eat it. Whole fruit fills you more than juice.
mango: Vitamin C and beta-carotene, with plenty of sugar. Eat in measured portions, ideally with a meal or protein.
papaya: Vitamin C and folate with modest sugar. Ripe papaya is a gentle fruit for digestion.
guava: Among the highest fruit sources of vitamin C and fibre. Eat the seeds and skin when you can chew them.
pomegranate: Fibre sits in the seeds, so eat them rather than juice. Sprinkle over yogurt or salads.
orange: Vitamin C and some folate. Eat the fruit, not just the juice, for the fibre. Vitamin C helps absorb iron from dal and greens eaten the same day.
pineapple: Vitamin C and manganese. Acidic, so it can irritate a sensitive mouth. Raw pineapple softens dairy-based marinades quickly.
watermelon: Mostly water with some vitamin C. Hydrating but low in protein and fibre, so it does not replace a snack.
cantaloupe: Rich in vitamin A from beta-carotene and in vitamin C. Wash the rind before cutting.
grapes: Quick sugar with little fibre. Best in small portions with a protein.
pear: Good fibre, much of it in the skin. Eat unpeeled.
strawberry: Vitamin C and low in sugar for a fruit. Wash just before eating.
blueberry: Low in sugar for a fruit and rich in polyphenols. Frozen berries are as nutritious as fresh.
avocado: Mostly unsaturated fat with fibre and potassium. Fat helps you absorb carotenoids from the vegetables you eat it with. Calorie dense, so about a quarter to a half per meal.
jackfruit: Fibre and vitamin C, but ripe jackfruit is sweet. Raw jackfruit works as a meat substitute but is low in protein.
lychee: Vitamin C with a lot of sugar. Eat fresh in season in small portions.
custard-apple: Energy-dense, sweet fruit with fibre and vitamin C. Remove the seeds, which are toxic if crushed.
sapodilla: Very sweet with fibre and some potassium. Eat fully ripe; unripe fruit is astringent.
tamarind: Souring agent, used in small amounts. Adds a little potassium and magnesium, not much else at normal use.
kiwi: Very high in vitamin C for its kcal. The skin is edible and adds fibre if you like it.
amla: One of the richest vitamin C sources. Heat and drying lower vitamin C, so fresh or lightly processed amla gives the most. Very sour: use in chutney or pickle.
raw-mango: Sour, with vitamin C. Use for chutney, dal and salads. Salt in the pickle is the main concern.
rolled-oats: Beta-glucan fibre, shown to lower LDL cholesterol, plus more protein than most grains. Soaking overnight makes oats softer; it does not add protein.
quinoa-dry: Complete protein, with more lysine than most grains. Rinse before cooking to remove bitter saponins. About 2.5x its weight when cooked.
atta-whole-wheat: Wholegrain, so more fibre, magnesium and B vitamins than maida. Fresh-milled atta spoils sooner; store airtight in a cool place.
maida-white-flour: Refined: most fibre and minerals removed. Use sparingly and combine with atta or besan.
semolina-suji: Refined wheat with little fibre. Dry roast before use for flavour. Add vegetables and a protein to make upma a full meal.
white-rice-dry: Quick energy with low fibre. Cool and reheat cooked rice to raise resistant starch a little; refrigerate quickly because cooked rice carries Bacillus cereus risk.
brown-rice-dry: More fibre and magnesium than white rice, but takes longer. Soaking for a few hours shortens cooking. Rinse and vary your rice, since rice can carry some arsenic.
jowar-flour: Gluten-free wholegrain with decent fibre and iron. Rotis need hot water in the dough to hold together.
cornmeal-yellow: Quick energy and some carotenoids. Low in protein: pair with beans or dairy, as makki roti with sarson does.
barley-pearled: Beta-glucan fibre, as in oats. Pearled barley is polished but still fibre-rich. Soak for faster cooking.
tapioca-pearls: Almost pure starch, with little protein or fibre. A fasting-day food; pair it with peanuts and yogurt.
buckwheat-groats: Gluten-free seed with good protein for a grain and rutin. Rinse well; roasted kasha has more flavour.
amaranth-grain: Higher in protein, calcium and iron than most grains. Cooks to a sticky porridge; mix with other grains for texture.
ragi-finger-millet: One of the best plant sources of calcium among grains. Fermenting or sprouting the flour reduces phytate and may improve mineral absorption.
poha-rice-flakes: Light and fast to make. Some brands are iron-fortified, so check the label. Rinse, do not soak long, and add peanuts, peas and paneer for protein.
bajra: Wholegrain with iron and magnesium. Warming and dense; pair with greens and dairy.
seviyan-wheat-vermicelli: Refined wheat that cooks in minutes. Dry-roast first. Low in protein, so add milk, nuts or paneer.
bulgur-dry: Pre-cooked cracked wheat, so just soak. More fibre than rice and ready quickly. Contains gluten.
bulgur-cooked: Ready to use in salads and tabbouleh. Cool before adding fresh herbs.
couscous-dry: Quick-cooking refined wheat pasta. Use whole wheat couscous for more fibre.
quinoa-cooked: Ready to add to salads and bowls. Keeps about 4 days in the fridge.
spaghetti-whole-wheat-dry: More fibre than white pasta and a similar cooking time. Cook until just firm: al dente raises blood sugar less than soft pasta.
pita-whole-wheat: A convenient wrap or scoop. Choose whole wheat for more fibre. Warm it so it stays flexible.
tortilla-corn: Often made with lime-treated corn (nixtamalised), which makes niacin available. Warm before using to prevent cracking.
tortilla-whole-wheat: A quick wrap base. Check the sodium on the label.
kidney-beans-dry: High in protein and fibre. Soak 8 to 12 hours, discard the water, then boil hard for at least 10 minutes: raw or undercooked kidney beans contain a toxin that causes illness.
chickpeas-dry: High in protein and fibre. Soak 8 to 12 hours and discard the water to reduce gas-causing sugars. Pair with lemon or tomato for iron absorption.
chickpeas-canned: Convenient and already cooked. Rinse well to remove up to about a third of the sodium.
black-beans-dry: High in fibre and folate. Soak and discard the water; boil thoroughly. Serve with a vitamin C source such as salsa or lime for iron.
black-beans-cooked: Ready to use. If canned, rinse to cut sodium. Keep cooked beans up to 4 days in the fridge.
pinto-beans-dry: Mild and creamy with good fibre. Soak and boil until fully soft.
lentils-green-brown-dry: Hold their shape, so good in salads. No soaking needed; they cook in about 25 minutes. High in iron and folate.
masoor-dal-dry: Cooks fast without soaking. Good iron and folate. Squeeze lemon on the finished dal to aid iron absorption.
moong-whole-dry: Easy to digest compared to most legumes, and sprouts well. Soak 6 hours to speed cooking.
toor-dal-pigeon-peas: Standard dal. Wash well and soak 30 minutes to cook faster. A tadka of cumin and hing eases digestion for many.
urad-dal-dry: Sticky and rich in protein and iron. Soak 4 to 6 hours for grinding into dosa and idli batter, where fermentation helps digestibility.
split-peas-dry: High in fibre and protein, cook to a thick soup or dal. No need to soak but cooking is quicker if you do.
soybeans-dry: Complete plant protein. Needs a long soak and thorough cooking. Raw soy contains trypsin inhibitors that cooking removes.
blackeyed-peas-fresh: Quick to cook and rich in folate. Fresh peas need only 15 to 20 minutes.
moong-sprouts: Lower in anti-nutrients than dry moong and add volume. Raw sprouts carry food-safety risk: cook them lightly, especially for children, older people and in pregnancy.
chickpea-sprouts-proxy-lentil-sprouts: This entry uses lentil sprout data as a stand-in. Sprouts add volume and vitamin C. Cook them lightly rather than eating raw.
chana-dal: Split Bengal gram, low glycaemic and high in protein and fibre. Soak 2 hours for faster cooking.
kala-chana: More fibre and iron than white chickpeas, with a firmer bite. Soak overnight and discard the water.
horse-gram: Traditional high-protein, high-iron pulse. Needs long soaking and cooking. Sprouted horse gram cooks faster.
moth-bean: Small, quick-cooking and protein-rich. Sprout or soak overnight.
lobia-brown-dry: Cooks faster than most beans. High in folate. Soak 2 to 4 hours if you want shorter cooking.
urad-dal-whole-ifct: Black gram with the skin on has more fibre. Soak overnight and cook long; it is rich and heavy.
navy-beans-dry: Mild and soft, with high fibre. Soak, discard water and boil until creamy.
great-northern-beans-cooked: Ready-to-use, good in soups and salads with kale. Rinse if canned.
lentils-green-brown-cooked: Ready to add to bowls. Keeps about 4 days in the fridge.
peanut-butter-natural: Protein and unsaturated fat, but very energy dense, so measure it with a spoon. Choose one with only peanuts and salt.
peanuts-dry-roasted: High in protein, and calorie dense, so a small handful. Check for added salt.
pumpkin-seeds: Good source of zinc and magnesium. Toast lightly for flavour and sprinkle over bowls, yogurt and salads.
hemp-seeds-hulled: Complete protein with omega-3 ALA. Eat raw on yogurt or salads; heat damages the delicate fats.
flaxseed: ALA omega-3 and fibre, but whole seeds pass through undigested. Grind fresh and keep in the fridge; ground flax goes rancid in warm cupboards.
chia-seeds: Fibre and ALA. Always soak or mix in liquid, never eat dry spoonfuls: they swell and can be a choking risk.
sesame-seeds: Calcium, iron and healthy fats. Ground or as tahini they are absorbed better than whole seeds. Toast for flavour.
sunflower-seeds: Vitamin E and magnesium. Use unsalted when you can.
watermelon-seeds: Magnesium and protein, usually eaten as roasted kernels. Small portion.
tahini: Ground sesame, so calcium and iron are easier to absorb than from whole seeds. Rich: use a spoonful in dressings and hummus.
almonds: Vitamin E, magnesium and fibre. Soaking mainly changes texture and taste, not nutrient absorption in any meaningful way. A small handful is a standard portion.
walnuts: The best common nut source of ALA omega-3. Store in the fridge so the fats do not go rancid.
cashews: Creamy and good for sauces when soaked and blended. Moderate protein, with iron and zinc.
pistachios: Good protein and potassium for a nut. Buying them in the shell slows down eating.
oil-mustard: Traditional in North and East Indian cooking. Heat until it stops smelling raw. Not suitable for all regions: erucic acid limits its sale as food in some countries.
oil-sesame: Toasted sesame oil is for flavour at the end; refined sesame oil can be used for cooking.
oil-coconut: Mostly saturated fat. Use in small amounts for flavour in South Indian dishes.
oil-olive: Mostly monounsaturated fat. Extra virgin is best raw or at moderate heat for dressings and light cooking.
oil-canola: Low in saturated fat with some ALA omega-3. A neutral oil for everyday cooking.
oil-sunflower: Mid-oleic sunflower oil is more stable than regular sunflower oil. Fine for shallow frying.
oil-peanut: Handles high heat well and tastes mild when refined. Avoid for anyone with a peanut allergy.
sugar-white: No nutrients other than kcal. Keep to a small amount, and not in everyday recipes.
sugar-brown: Nutritionally close to white sugar; the small mineral content is not meaningful.
honey: Counts as a free sugar. Traditional uses have little human evidence behind them. Do not give to infants under 1 year.
molasses-blackstrap: Contains some iron, calcium and potassium, but is still mainly sugar. Use a teaspoon in baking, not as a supplement.
vinegar-white: For pickling and sharp dressings. No notable nutrients.
cocoa-powder: Unsweetened cocoa is a source of fibre, iron and polyphenols. Use in oats and shakes without adding sugar.
papad: Light but salty, often fried. Roasting or microwaving uses less oil. Treat as a side, not a protein source.
jaggery: Mostly sucrose with small amounts of minerals. It still counts as sugar: use a little in treats.
olives-black: Healthy fats, but cured in brine so high in sodium. A few are enough for flavour.
mustard-prepared: Flavour with few kcal. Sodium varies: check the label.
soy-sauce-shoyu: High in sodium: a teaspoon has a lot. Use low-sodium soy sauce and cut back added salt. Wheat-based, so not gluten free.
maple-syrup: A free sugar with trace minerals. Use sparingly as a treat.
vinegar-red-wine: For dressings. A splash of vinegar in a dressing adds acidity that brightens bean and lentil salads.
vinegar-balsamic: Sweeter and thicker than other vinegars. Good drizzled over roasted vegetables.
tofu-extra-firm: Complete plant protein, with calcium when set with calcium sulfate. Super-firm tofu needs no pressing. Marinate after pressing, as it absorbs flavour like a sponge.
tempeh: Fermented soy with high protein and good fibre. Steam for 10 minutes before frying or marinating to reduce bitterness.
edamame-frozen: Complete protein and fibre in a convenient pod. Boil 4 to 5 minutes, season with salt and lime.
vital-wheat-gluten: Almost pure wheat protein, the base of seitan. Low in lysine, so combine with legumes or dairy. Not for coeliac disease or gluten sensitivity.
soya-chunks-proxy-defatted-soy-flour: Textured soy protein, very high in protein. Soak in hot water for 10 to 15 minutes, squeeze out, then season. The data here is a proxy from defatted soy flour.
edamame-prepared: Ready-to-eat cooked soybeans. Adds protein and fibre to salads and bowls.
turmeric-powder: Curcumin is poorly absorbed on its own; black pepper and fat help in lab and small human studies. Good as a flavour: the health claims are weaker than often stated.
cumin-seed: Dry-roast or temper in hot oil to bring out flavour. It adds flavour, not meaningful minerals, at spice-box amounts.
coriander-seed: Mild and citrusy. Toast and grind fresh for the best flavour.
mustard-seed: Pops in hot oil within seconds: add to the pan once the oil is hot and cover.
fenugreek-seed: Bitter, so use a small amount and do not burn it. Soaking mellows the flavour.
fennel-seed: Often chewed after meals traditionally. Evidence for digestion benefits is limited; it is a pleasant breath freshener.
black-pepper: Add near the end of cooking for the strongest flavour. Piperine can raise absorption of some compounds, such as curcumin.
chili-powder: Heat varies a lot between brands. Capsaicin gives the heat; the kcal and nutrients are small at use levels.
cayenne: Hot. Start with a pinch and add to taste.
paprika: Colour and mild flavour from carotenoids. Smoked paprika adds depth without heat.
cardamom-ground: Aromatic; lose flavour quickly once ground. Grind pods fresh where possible.
cinnamon-ground: Cassia cinnamon contains coumarin, which in large amounts is a concern for the liver. Ceylon cinnamon contains much less. A pinch in oats is fine.
cloves-ground: Very strong. A tiny pinch is enough; eugenol is the flavour compound.
nutmeg-ground: Use a pinch. Large amounts are toxic.
mace-ground: Milder than nutmeg, from the same fruit. Use sparingly in sweet and savoury dishes.
bay-leaf: Remove before serving: the leaf is not eaten.
curry-powder: A blend, so the content varies by brand. Check the salt content and fry it briefly in oil before adding liquid.
ginger-ground: More concentrated and a bit different in flavour from fresh. Fresh ginger works better in most Indian dishes.
saffron: A pinch soaked in warm milk for 10 minutes. Expensive and used in tiny amounts, so no nutritional contribution.
poppy-seed: Adds crunch and some calcium. Eaten in small amounts in curries and breads.
ajwain-proxy-caraway: Nutrition data here is for caraway as a stand-in for ajwain. Traditionally used to ease gas with dals and fried food.
garlic-powder: Convenient but milder than fresh, and with little of the allicin that forms when fresh garlic is crushed. Not suitable where onion and garlic are avoided.
onion-powder: Convenient flavour for dry rubs and bakes. Not suitable where onion and garlic are avoided.
anise-seed: Sweet, licorice flavour. Chew or add to teas and sweets.
dill-weed-fresh: Fresh dill is delicate: add at the end. Good in raita and with lentils.
coriander-leaf-dried: Weaker than fresh. Use fresh when you can; add dried early in cooking.
salt-table: Health Canada's upper limit is 2,300 mg sodium a day. Season at the end, taste first, and use iodised salt as part of your iodine intake.
baking-soda: A leavener. Too much leaves a soapy taste and destroys some B vitamins; measure carefully.
baking-powder: Leavening agent with some sodium. Use fresh: old baking powder loses its lift.
asafoetida: Used in tiny amounts in the tadka. Often cut with wheat flour, so check if you need gluten free.
cardamom-green: Whole pods give a milder flavour than ground. Crush the pod and use the seeds.
flax-linseeds-ifct: Same as flaxseed. Grind before eating; whole seeds pass through undigested.
oregano-dried: Adds flavour for almost no kcal. Rub between your fingers to release the oils.
thyme-dried: Good with beans and roasted vegetables. Add early in cooking.
whey-protein-powder: Complete protein. Optional: use it only to close a protein gap. Mix with milk or yogurt rather than water for taste and extra protein.
soy-protein-isolate: A plant-based protein powder. Optional. Blend well, as it can be gritty.
green-peas-fresh: Surprisingly high in protein and fibre for a vegetable. Frozen peas are as nutritious as fresh.
onion: Quercetin and prebiotic fibre. Fresh onion is mild, cooked onion is sweet. Not suitable where onion and garlic are avoided.
tomato: Cooking in a little oil raises lycopene availability. Fresh tomato adds vitamin C that helps iron absorption from lentils.
tomato-puree: Concentrated lycopene and convenient for curries. Choose no-salt-added versions.
tomato-paste: Highly concentrated: lycopene is best absorbed when cooked in oil. A spoonful goes a long way.
potato: Potassium and vitamin C, with the skin on for fibre. Cooling cooked potatoes increases resistant starch a little.
sweet-potato: Rich in beta-carotene, which absorbs better with fat. Bake or steam rather than frying.
spinach: Iron and folate, but oxalate limits calcium and some iron absorption. Cooking reduces oxalate; add lemon for vitamin C.
cauliflower: A cruciferous vegetable with vitamin C and fibre. Do not overboil: steam or roast instead.
cabbage-savoy: Vitamin C and K. Raw and lightly cooked cabbage keeps the most glucosinolates.
carrot: Beta-carotene is better absorbed when cooked and eaten with a little fat.
eggplant: Low in kcal, with fibre and a little potassium. It soaks up oil when fried: roast or air-fry instead.
okra: Fibre and vitamin C. The mucilage is reduced by cooking it dry first or adding acid.
bottle-gourd: Very hydrating and low in kcal. Cooks quickly. Rarely bitter: if it tastes bitter, discard it, as bitter gourds can contain toxic cucurbitacins.
bitter-gourd: Bitter taste is part of it. Salting and rinsing, or cooking with tamarind, softens the bite.
capsicum-green: Vitamin C, higher in red peppers. Add near the end to keep crunch.
green-chilli: Vitamin C and capsaicin. Seeds and membranes carry most of the heat.
mushroom-white: Low kcal, with B vitamins and some potassium. Cook through. Exposing mushrooms to sunlight can raise their vitamin D.
cucumber: Hydrating and very low kcal. Leave the skin on for fibre and vitamin K.
beetroot: Dietary nitrate and folate. Roasting or steaming keeps more than boiling. Can colour urine pink; this is harmless.
radish-daikon: Crunchy and low in kcal, with vitamin C. Salting draws out water for pickles.
turnip: Mild and cooks fast. Vitamin C and fibre. The greens are edible too.
pumpkin: Beta-carotene and potassium. Roast or steam; pair with a little fat.
green-beans: Fibre and vitamin K. Cook until tender-crisp to hold colour and vitamin C.
broccoli: Vitamin C and sulforaphane precursors. Chop and rest 10 minutes before cooking, and steam lightly rather than boil.
lettuce-romaine: Folate and vitamin K, with crunch. Wash well and dry before dressing so the dressing clings.
kale: Vitamin K, vitamin C and calcium that is relatively well absorbed. Massage with dressing or cook briefly to soften.
celery: Very low kcal and crunchy. Mostly water and potassium.
corn-sweet: Fibre and carotenoids; more starch than most vegetables. Cooking raises ferulic acid availability.
garlic: Crush or chop and rest 10 minutes before heating to let allicin form. Not suitable where onion and garlic are avoided.
ginger: Used for flavour and traditionally for nausea. Some trial evidence supports it for nausea; other claims are weaker.
spring-onion: Vitamin K in the green part. Add raw as garnish or briefly cooked.
coriander-leaves: Vitamin K and a little vitamin C. Add at the end: heat dulls flavour.
mint-fresh: Flavour and low kcal. Add at the end; it blackens when cut and left.
taro-arbi: Resistant starch and potassium. Always cook thoroughly: raw taro contains calcium oxalate that irritates the mouth.
yam-suran: Starchy with fibre. Needs thorough cooking, often with tamarind or lemon, to avoid throat itch.
plantain-raw: Resistant starch when green. Boil or steam rather than frying.
amaranth-leaves: Iron, calcium and vitamin A. Oxalate is high, so cook it and eat with lemon.
mustard-greens: Vitamin K and a peppery bite. Sarson ka saag is traditionally cooked a long time with makki flour.
beet-greens: Often thrown away, but rich in vitamin K, iron and potassium. Cook like spinach.
lotus-root: Crunchy and mildly sweet with fibre and vitamin C. Soak sliced root in water with a little lemon to keep it pale.
yardlong-beans: Fibre and vitamin C. Cook quickly like green beans.
pumpkin-leaves: Rich in folate and iron. Cook thoroughly and remove tough fibres.
lemon-juice: Vitamin C helps absorb non-heme iron from dal, beans and greens when added at the table. Best added at the end of cooking.
lime-juice: Same use as lemon: add at the end for vitamin C and to improve iron absorption from beans.
sun-dried-tomato: Concentrated flavour and lycopene, but often salty and packed in oil. Choose dry-packed and rehydrate.
methi-leaves: Iron, folate and slight bitterness. Salting and squeezing lowers the bitterness. Add dried methi to dough for flavour.
curry-leaves: Fry in oil briefly to release flavour. Calcium and iron are present but you eat very little.
ridge-gourd: Light and watery, cooks quickly. Peel the ridges and cook until soft.
drumstick: Vitamin C and fibre. Chew the pulp and discard the tough fibres.
drumstick-leaves: High in iron, calcium and vitamin A relative to most greens. Cook like spinach and add lemon.
cluster-beans: Fibre-rich and slightly bitter. Blanch before cooking to soften bitterness.
ash-gourd: Very low kcal and hydrating. Cooks to a soft texture in dals and curries.
snake-gourd: Mild and light. Cook until soft, often with grated coconut.
colocasia-leaves: Iron and vitamin A. Raw leaves cause throat itch: cook thoroughly, usually with tamarind or besan.
radish-leaves: Often discarded, but they hold more calcium and vitamin C than the root. Cook like other greens.
water-chestnut: Crunchy and low kcal. Boiled in the shell, it is a fasting-day food.
parsley-fresh: Vitamin K and vitamin C. Add fresh at the end, stems included in cooked dishes.
basil-fresh: Tear instead of cutting and add at the end. Heat dulls the aroma.
red-bell-pepper: Very high in vitamin C; more than green peppers. Eat raw or lightly cooked.
zucchini: Low kcal and mild, with potassium. Salt and drain to prevent soggy bakes.
arugula: Peppery and low kcal with vitamin K. Dress at the last moment or it wilts.
fennel-bulb: Crisp and aniseed-like, with fibre and potassium. Slice thinly for salads.
tomatoes-canned-whole: Canned tomatoes have more available lycopene than fresh. Choose no salt added.
water-tap: Used to loosen dips and dressings. List it in grams in a recipe so the batch weight is right. It adds no calories or protein, and it never goes on the shopping list.
hummus-commercial: Ready-made hummus for days you do not want to blend your own. Check the label for garlic and salt, and use it within a few days of opening.
